task_title: Communications, Light Signals, and Runway Lighting Systems
area: Area III. Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can find and set every frequency you need, talk and read back like a professional, use the transponder and radar services, read light gun signals, handle a radio failure VFR or IFR, read approach, runway and runway status lights, and decide when to declare an emergency and when to call the NTSB.
why: As a commercial pilot you will fly into busy and unfamiliar airports for pay. Clear radio work, a calm lost-comm plan and correct reading of airport lights keep you and your customers safe when things go wrong.

warmup: You are 12 miles from a towered airport at dusk. Tower stops answering, but your panel lights look normal. What are the first three things you check before you decide the radio has failed?

key_terms.def: Your first call to a facility, or to a new controller in the same facility: facility, full call sign, position if on the ground, request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1]].
"Repeat my message back to me." Pilots read back runways, hold shorts, altitudes and vectors [[34:404|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].
I have received your message, understand it, and will comply with it [[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]].
I can't comply with that specific instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]].
Your fuel lets you accept little or no undue delay at destination. Not an emergency, and it gets no priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].
Distress: serious or imminent danger, need immediate help (MAYDAY). Urgency: need timely but not immediate help (PAN-PAN) [[34:337|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:437|AIM P/C Glossary]].
Transponder code for loss of two-way radio communication [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].
ATC warning that you are unsafely close to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft, e.g., "Low altitude alert" [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]].
Tower signal light with an intense, narrow red, white or green beam, used when radio contact can't be made [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13a]].
Runway Status Lights: automatic red RELs and THLs that warn a runway is unsafe. They never replace an ATC clearance [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].
Precision approach path indicator: one row of 2 or 4 lights, normally left of the runway; 2 white and 2 red means on glide path [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].
FAA Aviation English Language Standard: communicate in English in a discernible and understandable manner, at least ICAO Level 4 [[10:1|AC 60-28B 1.1]] [[10:2|AC 60-28B 3]].

chunks.title: Find and set the right frequency

body.p: Commercial flying takes you to airports you don't know. Build your frequency list on the ground. Common sources are aeronautical charts, the Chart Supplement (the most complete airport information, revised every 56 days) and ATIS [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]].

On the sectional, towered airports and their data are blue; all others are magenta. The airport block gives the tower (CT) primary frequency, a star if the tower is part-time, a C symbol after the CTAF, the ATIS and the UNICOM [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].

head: You need
Where to find it
rows: Chart Supplement, instrument approach and departure charts, or ask any FSS [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9b3]]
Most are in the 121.6 to 121.9 MHz band [[33:257|AIM 4-3-14c]]
Chart Supplement and approach charts. It is not on the sectional [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8d]]
An FSS when unsure of the frequency
122.2 MHz, the common en route frequency for most FSSs [[33:235|AIM 4-2-14a]]
121.5 MHz, guarded by most civil towers and radar facilities [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1h]]

body.p: Your VHF radio tunes 118.000 to 136.975 MHz and needs 25 kHz spacing (e.g., 134.575) to use the whole system. If ATC assigns a frequency you can't select, ask for another [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

bullets: Store the next frequency in standby while one frequency stays active [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].
Select the right transmitter on the audio panel. Moving the selector from COM1 to COM2 changes both transmit and receive [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
Use the second radio to listen to ATIS while you stay with ATC on the first [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
After any change, pause and listen so you don't step on someone [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2a]].

callout.text: Write the list in the order you will use it: ATIS, Clearance or Ground, Tower or CTAF, Departure, then the same for your destination plus its PCL frequency.

check.q: Your night destination has pilot-controlled lights. Where do you find the frequency to click?
check.a: In the Chart Supplement or on the instrument approach chart. It is not printed on the sectional [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8d]].

chunks.title: Radio technique and the initial call

body.p: The single most important thought in pilot and controller talk is understanding. Acknowledge each call with your call sign. Be brief, but use whatever words you need to get the message across [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1b]].

bullets: Listen before you transmit; you may get what you need from ATIS or the frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2a]].
Think before you key. Jot down long messages, like an IFR position report [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2b]].
Mike close to your lips, a slight pause after pressing the button, normal tone [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2c]].
Wait a few seconds before calling again; the controller may be busy on another frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2d]].

body.p: Initial contact format: (a) facility name, (b) full call sign, (c) your position if on the airport surface, (d) your request or the type of message, (e) "Over" if required [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1]]. If reception is good, add your position, altitude and "information Charlie received," but don't overload the controller [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]].

callout.text: Example: "Miami Center, Baron Five Six Three Hotel, request V-F-R traffic advisories." [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1]]

body.p: Call signs: say the type, model or maker, then the registration, and drop the N ("Aztec Two Four Six Four Alpha") [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a3]]. Air taxi and other commercial operators without an FAA-authorized call sign add "Tango" in front: "Tango Aztec Two Four Six Four Alpha" [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a4]]. After contact, ATC may shorten your call sign to the prefix and last three characters, and then you may too [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]].

head: Item
Say it
rows: "one one niner point three five" [[33:233|AIM 4-2-8e]] [[33:233|AIM TBL 4-2-2]]

callout.text: Time is UTC ("Zulu"); say "local" for local time. From standard time add 5 (Eastern), 6 (Central), 7 (Mountain) or 8 (Pacific); in daylight time subtract 1 hour from those [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12, TBL 4-2-3]].

check.q: You fly Cessna N52917 for an air taxi company that has no FAA-authorized call sign. How do you identify on initial contact?
check.a: "Tango Cessna Five Two Niner One Seven": the Tango prefix, the maker, then the registration without the N [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a3-4]].

body.p: Good phraseology is the mark of a professional pilot. Jargon, chatter and "CB" slang have no place on ATC frequencies. The Pilot/Controller Glossary is the same glossary controllers use in FAA Order JO 7110.65 [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1c]].

head: Say
It means
rows: I received all of your last transmission. Never a yes or no [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Received, understood, and I will comply [[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Yes / No, permission not granted, or that is not correct [[34:302|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:385|AIM P/C Glossary]]
I can't comply with that instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Repeat your last transmission, or the part named [[34:413|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Request confirmation, e.g., "verify assigned altitude" [[34:438|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Pause a few seconds. It is not an approval or a denial [[34:420|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Over: I expect a response. Out: conversation ended, no response expected [[34:391|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:390|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Prompt action is needed to avoid an imminent situation [[34:342|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:362|AIM P/C Glossary]]

body.p: Acknowledge with your call sign at the start or end, plus Wilco, Roger, Affirmative, Negative or another fitting remark [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3c]].

callout.text: Phrases that cause trouble: "Traffic in the area, please advise" is not a recognized phrase [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g1]]. "Have numbers" means wind, runway and altimeter only, not the ATIS [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13h]]. Say the runway number, not "active runway" [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g8]].

check.q: Departure asks, "Verify you are climbing to one zero thousand." You are. What is the best reply?
check.a: "Affirmative, climbing to one zero thousand," plus your call sign. Roger does not answer a yes/no question [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]], and altitudes are read back [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: calls, readbacks and compliance

body.p: A towered-airport departure and return, the way an examiner wants to hear it:

head: Step
What to say or do
rows: Listen, note the letter, and on first contact say "information (letter) received" [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13c-d]].
Call sign, location, VFR or IFR, and first landing point: "Washington Ground, Beechcraft One Three One Five Niner at hangar eight, ready to taxi, I-F-R to Chicago" [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18d1]].

Always read back the runway assignment, any clearance to enter a runway, and any hold short or line up and wait [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]. A route to your runway does not let you enter or cross it [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]].
Stay on Ground through taxi and run-up unless told otherwise, then call Tower for takeoff [[33:257|AIM 4-3-14a]]. You need a clearance to taxi onto a runway, take off or land [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a4]].
Single pilot: once cleared onto the runway for departure, monitor only ATC until you are out of the Class B, C or D surface area [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b2]].
Acknowledge, then switch as soon as possible, unless told to change at a time, fix or altitude [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d-e]].
Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions and vectors in the order given, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b1]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b2]].
Establish two-way radio communication before you enter [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]]. Read back the runway in your landing clearance [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b4]].

body.p: Comply, or say so. If a situation demands your response, take action or tell the facility right away about any problem [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3c]]. Accepting or refusing a clearance is your responsibility [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7c]].

callout.text: If you are not sure of an ATC clearance, ask for clarification immediately. Once you accept a clearance, don't deviate unless it is amended, an emergency exists, or you are following a TCAS resolution advisory [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

check.q: Approach: "Cessna Four Kilo Lima, turn left heading two seven zero, descend and maintain three thousand." What do you say?
check.a: "Left heading two seven zero, descend and maintain three thousand, Cessna Four Kilo Lima": items in the order given, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b1]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b2]].

body.p: Your transponder answers radar with one of 4,096 four-digit codes [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20b1]]. Mode C or S and ADS-B Out also send your altitude in 100-foot steps [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20c1]]. ATC gives transponder instructions with the word "squawk" [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]].

head: When
Set
rows: Leaving parking, and anywhere on the movement area
Parked at the gate or ramp
Assigned code with altitude reporting (required) [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a4a]]; ADS-B Out transmitting at all times unless ATC says otherwise [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a4b]]
Emergency, not in contact with ATC

bullets: Press IDENT only when ATC asks [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20d]]. It is good practice to confirm out loud that you changed codes or pressed IDENT [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
When changing codes, don't pass through 7500, 7600-7677 or 7700-7777. Going from 2700 to 7200? Set 2200 first, then 7200 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]].
On initial contact, report your exact altitude to the nearest 100 feet [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c3]].

"Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs by (number) feet" may mean bad encoder data or a wrong altimeter setting, so check your altimeter [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c2]]. The Kollsman window does not change what the encoder sends [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
Coverage is line of sight; low altitude or antenna shielding can lose you, and climbing helps [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a8]].

callout.text: Mode C and ADS-B Out are required in Class A, B and C; above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class B or C up to 10,000 ft MSL; in Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 states and DC, except at and below 2,500 ft AGL; and within 30 miles of a Class B primary airport below 10,000 ft MSL (the Mode C veil) [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f2]]. The rules are 14 CFR 91.215, 91.225 and 99.13 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f1]].

check.q: Approach says, "Squawk VFR." What do you set?
check.a: Code 1200 in Mode A/3 (or another VFR code if one applies) [[1:359|PHAK Figure 14-43]] [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5a]].

body.p: Every terminal radar facility gives VFR pilots basic radar service: safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring when workload permits, and sequencing where it is set up [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18a1]].

head: Service
What you get
Your part
rows: Clock position, distance in miles, direction of travel, type and altitude if known [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15c1]]
Keep scanning. Advisories don't relieve you of see and avoid, and a busy controller may not give them [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15, 4-1-15b1]]
Warning of unsafe closeness to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft: "Low altitude alert, check your altitude immediately" [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]] [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16a1]]
Once it is issued, what to do is your decision [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]]
Automated low-altitude warning to the controller [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16a2]]
VFR with Mode C? Ask: "request MSAW monitoring" [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16a2]]
Vectors, when you can talk to the facility, are in coverage and radar identified [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17a]]
Vectors are advice. They never let you break a rule, and flying safely stays your job [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17b]]

bullets: Radar sees your track, not your heading. If you are holding a crab, called traffic will appear off to one side [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]].
Tell the controller the weather you're in and ahead, so you aren't vectored into IFR conditions [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17c]].
On VFR advisories, monitor the frequency all the time, report VFR altitude changes, and tell the controller before you leave; then squawk 1200 [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b2]].
VFR advisory service doesn't include vectors away from traffic unless you ask [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b2]].

callout.text: In difficulty VFR? If you are instrument rated and current in an IFR-equipped airplane, request an IFR clearance. If you are not and can't stay VFR, say you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b]].

check.q: A left crosswind has your nose pointed well left of your track. Approach calls traffic at 12 o'clock. Where do you look?
check.a: Right of the nose. ATC calls traffic from your track, and your nose is pointed left of it [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]].

body.p: The tower uses a light gun for aircraft without a radio, and for radio-equipped aircraft when contact can't be made. It sends an intense, narrow beam of red, white or green [[33:256|AIM 4-3-13a]] [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13a]]. The meanings are set in regulation [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].
Ask yourself first: am I on the surface or in flight? The same light means different things [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

head: Signal
On the surface
In flight
rows: Return for landing; steady green follows
Give way to other aircraft and keep circling
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return to starting point on airport

bullets: Limits: you may not be looking at the tower, and a light can only approve or disapprove what you seem to be doing [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13b]].
In flight, acknowledge by rocking your wings by day, or blinking landing or navigation lights at night [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].
On the ground, acknowledge by moving ailerons or rudder by day, or blinking landing or navigation lights at night [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].

At night on the ground, get the tower's attention with your landing light on, positioned clear of the active runway where the tower can see it. Leave it on until you get signals [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13c]].

callout.text: Steady green is the only full "go" (takeoff or land). Flashing green is one step short (taxi, or come back to land). Red means stop or keep away. White means go back where you started.

check.q: Holding short at night with a dead radio, you see alternating red and green from the tower. Can you take the runway?
check.a: No. It means exercise extreme caution. Only a steady green clears you for takeoff [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

chunks.title: Equipment problems that cut you off

body.p: Many "radio failures" are set-up errors or simple equipment problems. Check these before you squawk 7600.

head: Symptom
Likely cause and check
rows: Nothing heard for a long time
Volume, wrong frequency, or a stuck mike blocking the frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]]
A stuck mike, yours or another aircraft's; ATC may move everyone to another frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]]
You hear the station but it can't hear you
Out of range, or a remote site that transmits but doesn't receive on that frequency, often at VORs. Higher altitude increases VHF range [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2f]]
Hearing or talking on the wrong radio
Audio panel selection. The COM1/COM2 selector changes both transmit and receive [[23:53|IFH 2-2]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]
Radio lacks 25 kHz spacing; ask for another frequency [[23:53|IFH 2-2]]
Use a headset with the boom mike close to your lips [[23:53|IFH 2-2]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]
Charging failure: ammeter minus means more current used than replaced; full-scale minus means the alternator or generator has failed [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

body.p: After a charging failure, the battery may last about 30 to 40 minutes, but that is a rough number you can't rely on. Turn off what you don't need, pull circuit breakers if you must, and land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

bullets: Recheck your radios or use another transmitter, and keep the next call short [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]].
Call "ANY RADIO (tower) (station), GIVE (call sign) A CALL ON (frequency)," and say so if you have an emergency [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3b3]].
IFR: try the last assigned frequency, an FSS, or New York or San Francisco Radio, and 121.5. If you can, try them all at once [[34:54|AIM 6-4-3a]] [[34:55|AIM 6-4-3b]].

check.q: At night your ammeter shows full-scale minus. Home is 35 minutes away; a suitable towered airport is 10 minutes away. What is your plan?
check.a: The alternator has failed. Shed electrical load and land at the nearest suitable airport; 30 to 40 minutes of battery is only a guess [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]] [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

chunks.title: Lost communication procedures, VFR and IFR

body.p: Squawk 7600 when you lose two-way radio, and remember you may not be in radar coverage [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]. Whether a radio failure is an emergency is your call; 14 CFR 91.3(b) lets you deviate from any rule as needed to meet one [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1b]].

head: Arriving at a tower with
Do this
rows: Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the traffic flow. Then tell the tower your type, position, altitude, intention to land, and ask for light signals. At 3 to 5 miles, report position, join the pattern and watch for lights; on a full pattern, report downwind and base [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]].

Stay outside or above until you know the flow, join the pattern, monitor the tower frequency shown on the sectional, and look for lights. Acknowledge by rocking wings (day) or blinking landing or nav lights (night) [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].
Stay outside or above until you know the flow, join the pattern, and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]].

callout.text: VFR radio failure in Class D: you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land. Under IFR, follow 14 CFR 91.185 [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)]].

bullets: Radio dead before you leave the parking area? Get it fixed. If you can't, phone the tower and ask to depart without two-way radio [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]].
Busy airports don't accept no-radio arrivals [[1:357|PHAK 14-23]]. A quieter non-towered airport may be the wiser choice; watch extra carefully there [[1:358|PHAK 14-24]].

body.p: IFR, which most commercial applicants already fly: if the failure happens in VFR conditions, or you find VFR conditions after it, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. "Practicable" is not "possible": you don't have to land at an unsuitable airport or just minutes short of your destination [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1c2 Note]].

head: In IFR conditions
Fly
rows: Assigned; if vectored, direct to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance; then expected; then filed [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]]
The highest of: last assigned, the minimum IFR altitude, or the altitude ATC said to expect, for the segment being flown [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]

If the limit is a fix where an approach begins: start descent or the approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or if none, the ETA from your filed or amended time en route. If it is not: leave the limit at the EFC time, or on arrival if you have none, fly to an approach fix and start down as close as possible to the ETA [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]]

callout.text: Route: AVEF (Assigned, Vectored, Expected, Filed). Altitude: MEA (the highest of Minimum IFR altitude, Expected, Assigned).

check.q: IFR, your radio fails in IMC, then you break out into good VFR 10 miles from your destination. A small airport is 3 miles away. Must you land there?
check.a: No. Continue VFR and land as soon as practicable; you are not required to land minutes short of your destination [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]] [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1c2 Note]].

body.p: Airport beacons rotate or flash. White and green: lighted land airport. White and yellow: water airport. Green, yellow and white: heliport. Military airports show two quick white flashes between the greens. Airport beacons flash 24 to 30 times a minute [[33:132|AIM 2-1-9a]] [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9b-c]].

callout.text: A beacon on in daylight in a Class B, C, D or E surface area often means visibility under 3 miles or a ceiling under 1,000 ft. There is no rule that it must, so check the actual weather [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9d]].

head: Light
What you see
Why it matters
rows: Lights from the threshold out 2,400-3,000 ft (precision) or 1,400-1,500 ft (nonprecision); some have a "ball of light" racing toward the runway twice a second
Your transition from instruments to visual [[33:121|AIM 2-1-1]]
A pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the threshold
Finds the runway among city lights, low contrast or poor visibility [[33:126|AIM 2-1-3]]
White; on instrument runways, yellow on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less
Yellow is a caution zone for landing [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4a-b]]
Red toward the runway, green outward toward landing aircraft
Red: end for departures; green: threshold for arrivals [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4c]]
Every 50 ft; white, then alternating red and white for 2,000 ft, then all red for the last 1,000 ft
Tells you how much runway is left [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]]
Two rows of white bars from 100 ft to 3,000 ft or the midpoint, whichever is less
Shows the touchdown zone in low visibility [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5b]]
A row of pulsing white lights across the runway
Hold-short point when LAHSO is in effect [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5e]]
Edges blue, centerline green; lead-off lights alternate green and yellow
Yellow-green lead-off lights mean you are still in the runway area or ILS critical area [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10a-b]] [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5c]]
A pair of flashing yellow lights, or a row of yellow in-pavement lights, at the hold line
A row of red lights across the taxiway at the hold line
Used below 1,200 ft RVR. Never cross a red stop bar, even with a clearance [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10e]] [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e]]

body.p: At a towered airport the tower controls approach and runway lights. You may ask for them on or off, or brighter or dimmer [[33:129|AIM 2-1-7]].

check.q: Landing at night on a long precision runway, the centerline lights turn all red. How much runway is left?

chunks.title: Glide slope lights and pilot-controlled lighting

body.p: VASI: 2, 4, 6, 12 or 16 light units in bars. A 2-bar VASI gives one glide path, normally 3 degrees. A 3-bar VASI adds an upper path about 1/4 degree higher for high-cockpit aircraft. Some glide paths are as steep as 4.5 degrees for obstacles [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2a1-2]]. VASIs are visible 3 to 5 miles by day and 20 or more at night, with obstacle clearance within 10 degrees of centerline out to 4 NM. Don't start down until you are lined up with the runway [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2a4]].

PAPI: one row of 2 or 4 lights, normally on the left side. Visible about 5 miles by day and up to 20 at night, with obstacle clearance within 10 degrees of centerline out to 3.4 NM [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].

Tri-color VASI: one light; red below, green on, amber above. Useful range 1/2 to 1 mile by day and up to 5 miles at night. Sliding from green to red you may see a dark amber, so don't take it for "above" [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2c]] [[1:351|PHAK 14-17]]. Pulsating VASI: steady white (or alternating red and white) on path, steady red slightly low, pulsing red lower, pulsing white high; about 4 miles by day and 10 at night [[33:125|AIM 2-1-2d]].

callout.text: In Class D airspace, an airplane approaching a runway with a visual approach slope indicator must stay at or above the glide path until a lower altitude is needed for a safe landing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]].

head: Pilot-controlled lighting: key the mike
Result
rows: Medium or lower intensity (lower REIL or REIL off)
Lowest intensity available (lower REIL or REIL off) [[33:132|AIM TBL 2-1-3]]

bullets: Always key 7 times first, then adjust down. Lights stay on 15 minutes from the most recent activation [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8b-c]].
Receivers may be set to low sensitivity, so key again when you overfly the airport or just before the final segment of an approach [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8c]].
The frequency is often the CTAF, but not always. Check the Chart Supplement or approach chart [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8d]].

check.q: On a 2-bar VASI both bars are red. What does it mean and what do you do?
check.a: You are below the glide path. Fly up until the far bar is red and the near bar is white [[33:123|AIM FIG 2-1-2]] [[1:351|PHAK Figure 14-29]].

body.p: RWSL is fully automatic. It uses surveillance data to turn on red in-pavement lights when a runway is unsafe to enter, cross, take off from or land on. It is a separate safety layer: it never gives or replaces a clearance, and controllers may not even see the lights change [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].

head: Lights
Where
Turn red when
rows: Along the taxiway centerline from the hold line to the runway edge, plus one at the runway centerline [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b]]
High-speed traffic is on the runway, or an aircraft on final is within about 1 mile (adjustable) [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b, b2]]
Two rows beside the runway centerline lights, 1,500 ft long, starting 375 ft from the departure threshold [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]]
You are in position or rolling AND another aircraft or vehicle is on, or about to enter, the runway [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]]

bullets: Red RELs: stop at the hold line or stay stopped, and call ATC if your clearance conflicts [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b4]].
Red THLs: stop if you safely can, or stay stopped, and contact ATC. If stopping isn't safe, use your best judgment and call ATC as soon as possible [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c3]] [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6c3]].
Never cross illuminated red lights. Lights going out is not a clearance [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d3-4]].
Always tell the tower when you stop because of RWSL [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d2]].
Transponder and ADS-B on from leaving parking until shutdown at parking, so the system sees you [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d1]].
If the system is turned off, a NOTAM is issued and the ATIS updated [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6e2]].

check.q: You are cleared for takeoff and rolling at 15 knots when the THLs ahead turn red. What do you do?
check.a: Stop, since it is safe to do so at that speed, and tell ATC the lights conflict with your clearance [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c3]] [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d2]].

chunks.title: Declaring an emergency, and the NTSB

body.p: An emergency is a distress or an urgency condition [[34:340|AIM P/C Glossary]]. You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you are doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather, or anything else that could hurt flight safety. That is the time to ask for help, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]]. Delay has caused accidents and cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2b]].

head: Situation
What to say
rows: Fuel lets you accept little or no undue delay at destination
"Minimum fuel" after your call sign. Not an emergency, and no priority implied [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15a]]
Fuel is low enough that you need priority to land safely
Declare an emergency for low fuel and give fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15a5]]
PAN-PAN, preferably three times. Priority over all but distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c-d]]
MAYDAY, preferably three times. Absolute priority; it silences the frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c-d]]

bullets: Climb if you can, for better radio and radar coverage, but no unauthorized climbs in IFR conditions in controlled airspace except under 91.3(b) [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2a1]].
In contact with ATC? Keep your code. If not, squawk 7700 with Mode C [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

Message, preferably in this order: MAYDAY or PAN-PAN, station, call sign and type, problem, weather, intentions and request, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].
Then follow ATC's advice, ask when you don't understand, and don't change frequency unless you absolutely must [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2b]].

callout.text: In an in-flight emergency you may deviate from any Part 91 rule as needed, and send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)-(c)]]. If you deviate from a clearance, tell ATC as soon as possible. If ATC gave you priority, send a detailed report within 48 hours to the facility manager if asked [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)-(d)]].

body.p: NTSB. An accident is death or serious injury to anyone, or substantial damage to the aircraft, between boarding with intent to fly and everyone getting off [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Engine failure or damage limited to one engine, bent fairings or cowling, dented skin, small punctured holes, ground damage to propeller blades, and damage to gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes or wingtips is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].
Notify the NTSB immediately for an accident or any of these serious incidents [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]:

bullets: Flight control system malfunction or failure
A required flight crewmember unable to do normal flight duties because of injury or illness
In-flight fire, or an in-flight collision
Damage to property other than the aircraft estimated over $25,000 (repair cost, or market value if a total loss, whichever is less)
Release of all or part of a propeller blade, unless caused only by ground contact
Complete loss of information (not just flickering) from more than 50 percent of the electronic cockpit displays, such as the primary flight and navigation displays
An overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident

Serious injury includes a hospital stay over 48 hours starting within 7 days, most bone fractures, internal organ injury, and second- or third-degree burns or burns over 5 percent of the body [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Don't disturb wreckage except to remove injured or trapped people, protect it from more damage, or protect the public [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10(b)]].
File NTSB Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days of an accident, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing. An incident report is filed only if the NTSB asks [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15(a)]].

check.q: You are told to hold at your destination. If cleared now you could land, but you can't accept any more delay after that. You don't need priority yet. What do you tell ATC?
check.a: "Minimum fuel" after your call sign. It is not an emergency; if you later need priority, declare an emergency and give fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15a]].

chunks.title: Communication risk, non-standard phraseology and the English standard

body.p: The radio link between pilot and controller can break with surprising speed and disastrous results [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1a]].

head: Hazard
Mitigation
rows: Expectation bias: hearing the taxi route you expected, especially at your home airport [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]
Read back runways and hold shorts every time [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]; unsure of the route, ask for progressive taxi [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b3]]
Similar call signs on the frequency
Never shorten your call sign on initial contact or when similar ones are around; say "verify clearance for (call sign)" if in doubt [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1-2]]
Not allowed unless ATC authorizes it [[60:451|14 CFR 91.123(e)]]
Use P/C Glossary words; good phraseology is the mark of a professional [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1c]]
Acknowledge first, or ATC can't tell a radio failure from a missed call [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]]
Two pilots: one accepts a clearance and doesn't tell the other
Brief every clearance across the cockpit [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11c3]]

body.p: English. To be eligible for a commercial certificate you must read, speak, write and understand English [[60:310|14 CFR 61.123(b)]]. The FAA standard is that you communicate in English in a discernible and understandable manner with ATC, pilots and others who prepare and fly the aircraft, with or without the radio [[10:1|AC 60-28B 1.1]]. The minimum is ICAO Operational Level 4 [[10:2|AC 60-28B 3]].

bullets: Level 4 looks at pronunciation, structure, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and interactions [[10:2|AC 60-28B 4.1]] [[10:3|AC 60-28B 4.1]].
An evaluator may read you an ATC clearance or a weather report and ask you to explain it [[10:8|AC 60-28B A.2.3]].
If you don't meet the standard on a practical test, the test stops and you are referred to the FSDO [[10:9|AC 60-28B A.2.4.2]].
A limitation is possible only for a medical reason such as hearing loss, never for lack of fluency or an accent too strong to understand [[10:7|AC 60-28B A.2.1.3]].

callout.text: Level 4 interaction means you handle misunderstandings by checking, confirming or clarifying [[10:3|AC 60-28B 4.1]]. That is exactly what "say again" and "verify" are for.

check.q: At a big unfamiliar airport, Ground reads you a long taxi route and you are not sure you got it. What do you do?
check.a: Ask right away. Request clarification [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]] or progressive taxi instructions [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b3]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: tower tables and airport data

body.p: Build your frequency list from the chart before you start the engine. On the face of the chart, a towered airport shows CT and the primary tower frequency. The full set (tower, ground control, ATIS, radar approach) is in the tower table on the chart border, and times in it are local [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

Read each row left to right. The hours column tells you when the tower is open, and O/T means other times, often by NOTAM. A tower or ground entry can depend on the runway or on the approach direction, so pick the frequency that fits your runway, as at Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky. A row with ASR/PAR has a radar instrument approach. The ATIS shown on the chart face is the arrival frequency, and its hours may differ from the tower's [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

Class B, Class C and TRSA radar frequencies are in a second table. Where a facility has several frequencies, each is tied to a sector, so check which sector you are in before you call [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

For airports without a tower, read the data block. A circled C means the airport uses the CTAF. An italic frequency such as 122.95 is an aeronautical advisory station (UNICOM). ASOS/AWOS shows only when full-time ATIS is not available, and VFR Advsy appears when ATIS is not available and the frequency differs from the tower's. A star by CT means the tower is part-time, so check the table for hours [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p 15]]. Say the facility name, your full call sign and your request in standard form on each frequency.

check.q: The chart shows CT 118.3 with a star. You plan to arrive after dark. What do you check?
check.a: The star means the tower operates part-time. Check the hours in the tower table, and the NOTAMs, and if it may be closed, plan to use the CTAF [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p 15]] [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

scenario.title: Paid photo flight with a failing alternator
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot flying a Cessna 182 on a paid aerial photography job, VFR, with one photographer aboard. At dusk, 30 miles from your home Class D airport, the ammeter needle sits on the minus side and the low-voltage light comes on. Approach's voice is getting weaker. The photographer says, "Don't make a fuss, the boss hates paperwork."

questions.q: What is the ammeter telling you, and how long can you count on the battery?
questions.a: More current is being drawn than replaced; full-scale minus means the alternator has failed [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. The battery may give about 30 to 40 minutes, but don't rely on it. Shed load and land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

questions.q: Should you tell ATC? Does the photographer's comment change anything?
questions.a: Yes, tell them now. Doubt about your situation is already at least an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]], and whether radio failure is an emergency is your decision, not the passenger's [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1b]]. Paperwork is not a reason: a report is needed only if ATC or the FAA asks for one [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]] [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]].

questions.q: Your first call was, "Approach, 182, we've got a little electrical thing, gonna head on in." What was wrong, and what should you say?
questions.a: No full call sign and no clear problem or request [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1]] [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1c]]. Say PAN-PAN three times, then the station, call sign and type, alternator failure, intentions, position, altitude, fuel in minutes and people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].

questions.q: Eight miles out, the radio dies completely. What code, and how do you get into the Class D airport?
questions.a: Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]. Stay outside or above the surface area until you know the traffic flow, join the pattern and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]. You may land in basic VFR with visual contact and a steady green [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

questions.q: On downwind you see a steady red light. Then, after you land, the photographer asks whether you must call the NTSB. Answers?
questions.a: Steady red in flight: give way to other aircraft and continue circling [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. No NTSB call for a 182 with round-dial instruments: nobody was hurt, nothing was damaged, and in a small single-engine airplane an electrical failure is not on the immediate-notification list [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)]]. If your 182 had glass displays and more than half of them went completely dark, that would be a listed serious incident [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5(a)(9)]].

skills.do: Find every frequency you need (ATIS, Clearance or Ground, Tower or CTAF, Approach or Departure, PCL) from the chart and Chart Supplement, set each one on time and select the right COM on the audio panel. The ACS gives no number tolerance; the evaluator judges accuracy and timing.
skills.practice: Before each flight, build the list from the chart and Chart Supplement [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]]. In flight, preload the next frequency in standby [[23:53|IFH 2-2]] and say each one out loud as you flip it.

skills.do: Make every call in standard AIM and P/C Glossary form: facility, full call sign, position if on the ground, then the request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a1]], with numbers, altitudes and headings spoken correctly.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the calls for a whole flight, and review the P/C Glossary from time to time as the AIM recommends [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1c]].

skills.do: Acknowledge every call with your call sign, read back runways, hold shorts, altitudes and vectors, then comply promptly or say "unable." Follow the evaluator's simulated ATC instructions the same way.
skills.practice: Have your CFI play ATC with hold shorts, vectors and frequency changes. Read back in the order given [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b2]] and ask for clarification whenever you are unsure [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

quiz.q: Approach tells you to contact Tower on 118.35, but your old radio can only tune 118.30 or 118.40. What should you do?
options: Ask ATC for an alternative frequency
Use 118.30; it is close enough
Squawk 7600
Switch to 121.5
quiz.why: Without 25 kHz spacing you can't select that frequency, so ask for another one [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

quiz.q: Departure asks if you can climb to 8,500, but clouds are in the way and you are VFR. Which word fits best?
options: Roger
Wilco
Stand by
Unable
quiz.why: "Unable" means you can't comply with a specific instruction or request [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]. Wilco promises to comply [[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]], and Roger only means you heard it [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]].

quiz.q: How do you say 13,500 feet on the radio?
options: Thirteen thousand five hundred feet
"One three thousand five hundred"
"One three five zero zero"
"Flight level one three five"
quiz.why: Below 18,000 ft, say the separate digits of the thousands plus the hundreds [[33:233|AIM 4-2-9a]]. Flight levels start at FL 180 [[33:233|AIM 4-2-9b]].

quiz.q: Approach says, "Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs by four hundred feet." What should you check first?
options: Your heading indicator and its compass setting
Your transponder code
Your altimeter setting
Your ADS-B In display
quiz.why: That call may mean bad encoder data or a wrong altimeter setting, so verify your altimeter is set correctly [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c2]].

quiz.q: It is night, your radio is dead, and you are on the ramp of a towered airport. How do you get the tower's attention?
options: Flash your nav lights from the ramp
Show a landing light and taxi clear of the active runway in view of the tower
Taxi onto the active runway and hold there until the tower sends a light signal
Squawk 7700 and wait
quiz.why: Turn on a landing light and taxi to a spot clear of the active runway where the tower can see the light; leave it on until you get signals [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13c]].

quiz.q: Near a VOR, you clearly hear the FSS on a frequency, but it never answers your calls. What is a likely reason?
options: The remote site transmits on that frequency but doesn't receive on it
Your receiver has failed
FSS ignores VFR calls
Your transponder is in standby
quiz.why: Remote sites don't always transmit and receive on all frequencies, especially at VORs, so you can hear but not reach the station [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2f]].

quiz.q: IFR in IMC, you are being radar vectored to join V23 when two-way radio fails. Which route do you fly?
options: The route filed in your flight plan, flown from your present position to the destination
Direct to V23, as given in the vector clearance, then as cleared
Back to the departure airport
Hold where you are until your ETA
quiz.why: If being radar vectored, fly direct from the point of failure to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(ii)]].

quiz.q: You keyed the pilot-controlled lights 7 times 10 minutes ago while overhead. Now you're starting the final segment of the approach. What should you do?
options: Nothing; they stay on until you land
Key 7 times again
Key 3 times to turn them off and on
Call UNICOM to keep them on
quiz.why: Key the mike as directed just before the final segment, even if the lights are on. It makes sure you're close enough and gives a full 15 minutes [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8c]].

quiz.q: What must happen for Takeoff Hold Lights to turn red?
options: Only your aircraft being on the runway
The tower controller switching them on by hand whenever a conflict is seen on or near the runway
You are in position or rolling and another aircraft or vehicle is on or entering the runway
Visibility below 1,200 ft RVR
quiz.why: THLs need two users: the departing aircraft in position or rolling, and another aircraft or vehicle on or about to cross the runway [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]].

quiz.q: Which of these, by itself, requires immediate NTSB notification?
options: A blown tire on landing
A propeller blade separates in flight
A dented cowling after a hard landing
An alternator failure
quiz.why: Release of all or part of a propeller blade, not caused only by ground contact, is a listed serious incident [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5(a)(8)]]. Tire and cowling damage are not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

quiz.q: Which airport in the table shows a radar instrument approach with ASR only?
options: Bolton
Charlottesville-Albemarle
Cox Dayton Intl
Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky Intl
quiz.why: Its row shows ASR in the last column. Bolton has ASR/PAR, Charlottesville has PAR, and Cox Dayton has none [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: What ATIS frequency is listed for Charlottesville-Albemarle?
quiz.why: The ATIS column for that row reads 118.425. 124.5 is the tower and 121.9 is ground [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: What are the tower hours at Eastern WV Rgnl/Shepherd on Sundays?
quiz.why: Its row lists 1300-1800 SUN. The Monday-to-Saturday hours are different, and O/T is by NOTAM [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: The italic number 122.95 under an airport's elevation is what?
options: The AWOS frequency used at that airport
The ATIS frequency used at that airport
The control tower frequency for the field
An aeronautical advisory station (UNICOM)
quiz.why: The legend lists italic 122.95 as the aeronautical advisory station [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p 15]].

quiz.q: You are in flight and a steady red light shows from the tower. What does it mean?
options: Cleared to land and exit at the first taxiway
Return for landing and expect a green light
Airport unsafe, do not land until further notice
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
quiz.why: For aircraft in flight, steady red means give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red means the airport is unsafe [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

takeaways: Build your frequency list on the ground from the chart, Chart Supplement and ATIS; the PCL frequency is not on the sectional.
Standard words prevent mistakes: Roger is not yes, and Unable, Verify and Say again clear up doubt.
Read back runways, hold shorts, altitudes and vectors, with your call sign.
Light gun: decide surface or flight first; steady green is the only full clearance.
Lost comm: troubleshoot, squawk 7600, stay out until you know the flow; IFR follows 14 CFR 91.185.
Red RWSL means stop even with a clearance; lights going out is not a clearance.
Doubt means urgency; minimum fuel is not an emergency; know the 49 CFR 830.5 list.
cfi_notes: Source differences (lesson follows the AIM and regulations): PHAK 14-18 calls the runway-edge caution zone amber and says runway end lights are red; AIM 2-1-4 says yellow, and red toward the runway with green outward. PHAK 14-23 says acknowledge at night by blinking the landing light; AIM 4-2-13a2 says landing or navigation lights. 14 CFR 91.125 says "cleared to taxi"; AIM TBL 4-3-1 and PHAK Figure 14-42 say "cleared for taxi."

IFH 2-3 says altitude reporting is required in Class B and C and within 30 miles of a Class B primary airport. The current AIM 4-1-20f list is longer (Class A, above Class B and C, Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL) and includes ADS-B Out. Teach the AIM list.
PHAK 14-19 gives RWSL status as of 2016 (14 airports). Treat it as dated; tell students to look for RWSL notes on airport diagrams and in NOTAMs.

Commercial checkrides often probe: minimum fuel versus an emergency for low fuel (AIM 5-5-15), "land as soon as practicable" versus "possible" (AIM 6-4-1 Note), and the Tango prefix for air taxi call signs (AIM 4-2-4a4).
Drill light gun signals by column: surface first, then in flight. Students most often swap flashing green (taxi / return for landing) with flashing red (clear the runway / do not land).
Run a real lost-comm drill: turn the volume down in flight (safely) and have the student troubleshoot, squawk 7600, plan the Class D entry and say the light signals out loud.

The English standard is evaluated all through training, not just on the checkride; instructors share responsibility for monitoring it (AC 60-28B 5.1). Practice by reading a clearance aloud and having the student explain it (AC 60-28B A.2.3).
gaps: K6: the sources give general radio and electrical checks but not aircraft-specific troubleshooting (headset jacks, a failed push-to-talk switch, avionics master, audio panel fail-safe mode). Use the POH/AFM.
The current list of RWSL airports is not in these sources; PHAK 14-19 is dated 2016.
ADS-B Out detail (AIM 4-5-7) and the full text of 14 CFR 91.215 and 91.225 are not covered; the lesson uses the AIM 4-1-20f summary.

The Chart Supplement itself is not in the source set; frequency lookup is taught from the PHAK, AIM and Chart Users' Guide.
The Skills elements have no numeric ACS tolerances; the evaluator judges standard phraseology and compliance.

activities.title: Light gun: true or false
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A flashing green light to an aircraft in flight means cleared to land.
cards.why: No. It means return for landing; a steady green will follow at the proper time [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

cards.s: A steady red light to an aircraft on the ground means stop.
cards.why: Yes. Steady red on the surface means stop [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

cards.s: A flashing white light has no meaning for an aircraft in flight.
cards.why: Yes. Flashing white means return to starting point on the airport, and is not applicable in flight [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

cards.s: A light signal can tell you which runway to use.
cards.why: No. Lights can only approve or disapprove what you appear to be doing; they carry no added information except the general warning signal [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13b2]].

cards.s: On the ground in daylight, you acknowledge a light signal by moving the ailerons or rudder.
cards.why: Yes. By day move the ailerons or rudder; at night blink the landing or navigation lights [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].

cards.s: A flashing red light in flight means give way to other aircraft and keep circling.
cards.why: No. That is steady red. Flashing red in flight means the airport is unsafe, do not land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

activities.title: No answer from the tower
activities.intro: You are flying N735CP, a Cessna 182, home from a paid photo flight. It is good VFR, and you are 15 miles from your Class D airport at 3,500 ft. Approach has just handed you off to Tower.

steps.s: Tower doesn't answer your first call. The radio display looks normal.
options: Squawk 7600 at once and enter the Class D, because one unanswered call proves the radio has failed
Check volume, frequency and the audio panel, then try again with a short call
Switch to 121.5 and declare a MAYDAY
Keep going and land without a clearance
steps.why: Check volume and frequency and make sure the mike isn't stuck [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]]; then recheck the radios or use the other transmitter, keeping the next call short [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]].

steps.s: Still nothing on COM1 or COM2, and you hear no other traffic at all. The electrical system looks fine. You are 10 miles out.
options: Circle over the field at pattern altitude until a light shows
Fly straight in to the runway you used for departure
Squawk 7700 and descend into the pattern
Squawk 7600 and stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the traffic flow
steps.why: Squawk 7600 for loss of two-way radio [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]. With a suspected dead receiver, stay outside or above the surface area until the direction and flow of traffic is known [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]].

steps.s: From outside the surface area you see the windsock and an airplane landing Runway 27. You think only the receiver failed.
options: Transmit in the blind: type, position, altitude, intention to land, and request light signals
Say nothing; if the receiver is dead the transmitter must be too
Call Ground instead of Tower
Fly low over the tower and rock your wings
steps.why: With a dead receiver, tell the tower your type, position, altitude and intention to land, and ask to be controlled with light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]].

steps.s: About 4 miles out you report your position and join a left downwind for Runway 27. On downwind the tower flashes a green light at you.
options: Land now on the runway in use, because any green light clears you to land from the pattern
Leave the pattern; the airport is unsafe
Stay in the pattern and expect a steady green; it means return for landing
Return to your starting point
steps.why: Flashing green in flight means return for landing, to be followed by steady green at the proper time [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Keep watching the tower for lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]].

steps.s: On final you get a steady green. The weather is good VFR and you can see the tower. May you land?
options: Yes, with basic VFR, the tower in sight, and a clearance to land
Only if you declared an emergency first
Only after rocking your wings twice
No; the tower must give you a spoken clearance to land on the frequency in use
steps.why: With a VFR radio failure in Class D you may land with basic VFR weather, visual contact with the tower and a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]]. Steady green in flight is that clearance [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

activities.title: Runway lights by the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A 9,000-ft precision runway has centerline lights. How many feet from the landing threshold do the centerline lights start alternating red and white?
items.why: Centerline lights are white until the last 3,000 ft: 9,000 - 3,000 = 6,000 ft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]].

items.q: On that same 9,000-ft runway, how many feet from the landing threshold do the centerline lights turn all red?
items.why: All centerline lights are red in the last 1,000 ft: 9,000 - 1,000 = 8,000 ft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]].

items.q: An instrument runway is 3,600 ft long. How many feet at the far end have yellow edge lights?
items.why: Yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less. Half of 3,600 = 1,800, which is less than 2,000 [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4b]].

items.q: A 5,000-ft precision runway has touchdown zone lights. How many feet beyond the landing threshold do they end?
items.why: TDZ lights run from 100 ft to 3,000 ft or the runway midpoint, whichever is less. Midpoint = 5,000 / 2 = 2,500 ft, less than 3,000 [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5b]].

final_quiz.q: It is 1520 Central Daylight Time. What UTC time do you use on the radio?
final_quiz.why: Central Standard Time is UTC minus 6, and in daylight time you subtract 1 hour from that: add 5. 1520 + 5 hours = 2020Z [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12, TBL 4-2-3]].

final_quiz.q: You fly Bonanza N3462T for an air taxi company that has no FAA-authorized call sign. How do you identify on first contact?
options: "Bonanza Three Four Six Two Tango"
"Tango Bonanza Three Four Six Two Tango"
"Six Two Tango"
"November Three Four Six Two Tango, Bonanza air taxi"
final_quiz.why: Air taxi operators without an FAA-authorized call sign put "Tango" before their normal identification: type, then the registration without the N [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a3-4]]. Never shorten it on initial contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1]].

final_quiz.q: Ground: "Cessna Niner Romeo Tango, Runway 34 Left, taxi via Bravo, cross Runway 27, hold short of Runway 34 Right." Which readback is correct?
options: "Wilco, Romeo Tango"
"Taxi via Bravo and hold short of the runways ahead, Cessna Niner Romeo Tango"
"Roger, Cessna Niner Romeo Tango"
"Runway 34 Left, cross 27, hold short 34 Right, Cessna Niner Romeo Tango"
final_quiz.why: Read back the runway assignment (with left or right), any runway crossing or entry clearance, and any hold short [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b4]], with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b1]].

final_quiz.q: You are on VFR flight following and want to leave to land at a non-towered airport. Approach hasn't said anything yet. What do you do?
options: Tell Approach before leaving the frequency, then squawk 1200
Switch to the CTAF without a word; Approach will drop you from radar on its own
Squawk 7600 so Approach knows you left
Stay on Approach until you land
final_quiz.why: When you no longer want advisory service, tell the controller before changing frequencies, then change your code to 1200 [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b2]]. Leaving silently looks like a radio failure [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]].

final_quiz.q: At night the ammeter shows full-scale minus and the low-voltage light is on. Your destination is 50 minutes away; a suitable airport is 12 minutes away. What should you do?
options: Continue; the battery lasts about an hour
Turn the master off and continue without lights
Shed electrical load and land at the nearest suitable airport
Climb to 12,000 ft for better radio range and continue to the destination
final_quiz.why: Full-scale minus means the alternator has failed [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. Battery life is roughly 30 to 40 minutes at best; never continue the flight. Shed load and land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

final_quiz.q: IFR, your radio fails in IMC at an assigned 6,000 ft. The next segment's MEA is 8,000 ft, and the one after that is 5,000 ft. No expected altitude was given. What altitude do you fly on the last segment?
final_quiz.why: Fly the highest of the last assigned altitude, the minimum IFR altitude and the expected altitude, for each segment [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]. On the last segment: higher of 6,000 assigned and 5,000 MEA = 6,000 ft, just like the AIM example [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1 Example 1]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing out with a dead radio, you see a flashing red light from the tower. What do you do?
options: Return to the ramp
Stop and wait for the tower's green light
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Continue to the run-up area
final_quiz.why: Flashing red to an aircraft on the surface means taxi clear of the runway in use. Stop is steady red; return to starting point is flashing white [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

final_quiz.q: At night you approach an unfamiliar airport in a bright city. You spot a pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of a runway end. What are they?
options: Runway guard lights
The airport beacon
Sequenced flashing lights leading up to the runway threshold
Runway end identifier lights (REIL)
final_quiz.why: REILs are a pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the threshold. They help find a runway surrounded by other lights [[33:126|AIM 2-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: Flying a tri-color VASI, you see the light change from green to a dark amber as you descend. Where are you?
options: Above the glide path, where amber shows
On the glide path
Going below the glide path, toward red
Far left of centerline
final_quiz.why: Descending from green to red you may see a dark amber in the transition [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2c Note 2]]. Don't mistake it for the above-glidepath amber [[1:351|PHAK 14-17]].

final_quiz.q: You are holding short of a runway with RWSL. The red RELs go out right after a landing airplane passes. You have no crossing clearance yet. What now?
options: Hold short until ATC clears you to cross
Cross if you can see no traffic
Flash your landing light and cross
Cross; dark lights mean the runway is clear
final_quiz.why: Don't proceed when lights go out without an ATC clearance. RWSL verifies a clearance; it never replaces one [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d4]]. A clearance is needed to cross any runway [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a5]].

final_quiz.q: In a holding pattern, you realize your fuel now requires priority handling to land safely. What should you do?
options: Squawk 7600
Say "minimum fuel" and keep holding until ATC offers a priority approach
Declare an emergency for low fuel; give fuel remaining in minutes
Wait until you are below 30 minutes of fuel
final_quiz.why: Minimum fuel implies no priority. If you need priority to land safely, declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15a4-5]].

final_quiz.q: On a charter flight, turbulence breaks a passenger's arm. The airplane is not damaged. What does 49 CFR 830 require?
options: Notify the NTSB immediately and file a report within 10 days
Nothing, because the airplane wasn't damaged and no one was killed
File a report only if the NTSB asks
Tell the nearest FSDO within 48 hours
final_quiz.why: A broken arm is a serious injury (any bone fracture except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose), so this is an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Accidents need immediate notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] and Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15(a)]].

final_quiz.q: On your commercial practical test, the examiner reads you a clearance and finds you can't explain it in English well enough to meet the standard. What happens?
options: You get a certificate limited to flights with a CFI
The test continues, and English is retested later
You take a written English test at a testing center
The test stops and you are referred to the FSDO
final_quiz.why: If an evaluator finds you don't meet the AELS during a Part 61 practical test, the test does not continue and you are referred to the FSDO [[10:9|AC 60-28B A.2.4.2]]. Limitations are given only for medical reasons [[10:7|AC 60-28B A.2.1.3]].

final_quiz.q: You are instrument rated and current, flying VFR in an IFR-equipped airplane on flight following, when the clouds close in around you. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Declare a distress condition as a non-instrument pilot would
Keep going VFR and ask for vectors through the clouds
Squawk 7700 and descend
Request an IFR clearance
final_quiz.why: An instrument-rated, current pilot in an equipped airplane should say so by requesting an IFR clearance [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b3]]. ATC vectors never let you break a rule, such as flying VFR into clouds [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17b]].

final_quiz.q: Which frequency is the tower frequency for runway 18L/36R at Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky Intl?
final_quiz.why: The tower column lists 118.975 360.85 for RWY 18L/36R, and 118.3 for the other runways shown [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

final_quiz.q: When does the chart show ASOS/AWOS and its frequency beside an airport?
options: When the airport has a control tower
When the airport is military
Only at night when the tower is closed
When full-time ATIS is not available
final_quiz.why: The legend says it is shown when full-time ATIS is not available [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p 15]].

final_quiz.q: ATC gives you a clearance, but you are not sure what it said. What does 91.123 tell you to do?
options: Read back what you think it was and comply
Continue as planned until it is repeated
Immediately ask ATC to clarify it
Ignore it, since VFR flights are not bound by clearances
final_quiz.why: When a pilot is uncertain of an ATC clearance, the pilot shall immediately request clarification [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].
